entries.title: Strait of Hormuz still a source of leverage for Iran
entries.summary: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz put crews at risk and drive up energy shipping costs. Iran's ability to sustain them and the limits of US protection will shape how much trade can continue and at what price.
entries.content:
Asia

Strait of Hormuz still a source of leverage for Iran

November 9, 2026

Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz put crews at risk and drive up energy shipping costs. Iran's ability to sustain them and the limits of US protection will shape how much trade can continue and at what price.

Since the Iran war started, attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz have put crews at risk of death and injury, forcing shipping companies to choose whether to attempt the passage or delay cargoes and face higher costs.  

Merchant vessels continue to use the strait despite the danger but how long that can continue depends partly on Iran's ability to sustain its attacks and the United States' capacity to protect shipping and bear the cost.

Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, believes Iran's geography and the equipment it uses allow it to keep attacking ships.

But he sees the economic burden of the war as Tehran's main constraint.



"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," he said.

It's unclear how long Iran can sustain attacks given the lack of reliable information on the nation's weapons stocks and its ability to replenish supplies. And sporadic attacks in the crucial waterway are also different from closing the strait completely.



"Even if a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz were possible, it would not be sustainable because it could carry high political costs for Iran," Mohammadi told DW. "Iran cannot indefinitely disrupt its allies' access to the strait."



By threatening shipping, Iran can raise the cost of confrontation and seek leverage in negotiations but that may not guarantee success or yield concessions, the expert said. 

More crossings, but traffic remains depressed

Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center's (UKMTO) weekly report, released on November 6, show 325 reported transits through Hormuz between October 29 and November 4. That was up from 277 the previous week, an increase of about 17%.

It's still roughly 65% below pre-war levels, the UKMTO assessed.

But vessel numbers alone cannot explain what is happening to energy supplies as cargo volumes and the routes used also matter, said Dalga Khatinoglu, an expert on Iran's energy and macroeconomics.

"If we look only at crude oil, Middle Eastern exports across all routes, from the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, have largely recovered to pre-war levels," he told DW. "In some weeks in September and October, they even exceeded those levels."

His assessment covers the region's overall crude exports across all routes, not just shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

The picture for refined petroleum products is different, Khatinoglu said. "Before the war, the Middle East exported about 6.2 million barrels of petroleum products a day. That figure has now roughly halved."



Liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports have also suffered. "As of September, exports from Qatar and the UAE were about 10% below pre-war levels. Although there has been some improvement, they remain severely disrupted," the expert underscored.

The cost of getting through spikes

Khatinoglu said recovering energy exports have not eliminated the costs associated with ongoing insecurity.

"Although oil exports from Middle Eastern countries have approached pre-war levels, shipping and insurance costs have remained very high," he stressed.

Citing recent figures from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), he said that average freight rates for a large tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia has risen about 12 times, from $3.18 (€2,84)  per barrel at the beginning of the year to $37.13 a barrel at the end of October.

This means elevated costs for Asian importers even when crude is available.

Reducing costs and restoring commercial confidence in the safety of the strait requires more than a US military presence, Mohammadi said.

"There is only one solution to the Strait of Hormuz issue and that's an end to the war, accompanied by a lasting agreement that brings lasting security," he said.

Khatinoglu shared a similar view. "You cannot expect oil prices to return to pre-war levels simply by relying on US protection for ships in the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

entries.title: Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault convictions
entries.summary: The former comedian was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others last week. The judge referred to Brand as a "predator."
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

The former comedian was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others last week. The judge referred to Brand as a "predator."

British media personality Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment on Monday after being found guilty of rape and assault. 

He is required to spend at least two-thirds of that time in prison, and may be released under supervision after that if he displays good conduct while in jail.

Judge Joel Bennathan called Brand a "predator," and said that the sentence is "just and proportionate...to the overall gravity of your criminality."

Bennathan also praised the "determination and bravery" of the survivors who came forward.

The 51-year-old had consistently denied the charges, brought about by six victims on allegations going back as far as 1999.

A jury of four women and eight men did not find his defense that all the encounters were consensual to be plausible, and found him guilty of raping or sexually assaulting four of his accusers.

What did Russell Brand's survivors say about him?

At the sentencing hearing, some of his victims gave victim impact statements to the court.

"I wanted ‌to express how this crime has affected me over the years," one woman said from behind a screen to protect her privacy, adding that the attack led to an "undeserved feeling of shame" she had carried for 20 years.

Another survivor called Brand a "sexual predator who has no remorse."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the bravery of the survivors in a statement, and said his government would be "relentless in making whatever improvements we can” to provide more support for victims and make sure every police station has a sexual assault response team.

Who is Russell Brand?

Brand rose to prominence in the UK stand-up scene in the early 2000s with sets focused on his sex life, alcoholism, and heroin addiction.

He then became a presenter for several British television shows before starring in several Hollywood movies and being in a brief, high-profile marriage to American pop star Katy Perry.

As accusations of predatory behavior toward women began to mount, Brand left London and Hollywood behind for Florida. His politics changed from left-wing activism to promoting conservative ideas and conspiracy theories on his podcast.

He has said he underwent a religious conversion around this time. In 2016 he resumed his relationship with restauranteur Laura Gallacher, whom he first dated in 2007 when he was 31 and she was 19. They have since had three children together. Gallacher has remained by Brand's side throughout the court proceedings.

entries.title: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?
entries.summary: Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences. 

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Winter shoes? Candy!

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

Stasi's photo treasure trove

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

What does the future hold?

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future." 

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany: CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president
entries.summary: The steering committtee of the CDU have announced Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner as presidential candidate. This gives her a good chance of becoming the first woman to occupy the role.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president

November 9, 2026

The steering committtee of the CDU have announced Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner as presidential candidate. This gives her a good chance of becoming the first woman to occupy the role.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday confirmed that they would be putting forward Ilse Aigner as a candidate to be Germany's next head of state. 

Aigner's own CSU, the CDU's Bavarian sister party, already supports her candidacy — and the federal coalition partners the Social Democrats have also made clear they would endorse her nomination if the conservatives agree on it. 

This means the 61-year-old has a good chance of taking up the largely ceremonial role when the special committee that elects a German president convenes in late January.

While Angela Merkel famously served as the country's most powerful politician for more than a decade, Germany has never had a female head of state.

What did Merz say about the nomination in Berlin?

Chancellor Merz announced the decision alongside Aigner at a Berlin press conference around 1 p.m. local time in the CDU's Konrad Adenauer House.

Merz said the "multifaceted, ambivalent" date of November 9 — anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall and the Nazi-led November pogroms — symbolized both "democratic hope and regained freedom, as much as the failure of democracy and the most serious crimes in our history that followed from it."

Merz said he and Aigner had known each other for decades, praising her human qualities like empahty and openness as well as her "pronounced engagement for parliamentary democracy."

"In Isle Aigner, the Federal Republic of Germany would gain a president with dignity and with heart, a president who would unite, provide orientation and initiate debates," Merz said in summation, referring to some of the roles traditionally seen as most crucial for a less partisan head of state not bound by the day-to-day battles of parliamentary politics.

How did Aigner respond?

Aigner, meanwhile, said she was "very moved" by the nomination, thanking various voices in the conservatives and beyond for their words of support in recent weeks. Given the strength of populist parties on both the right and left at present, Aigner said she wanted to prove worthy of support from Germany's more centrist groups.

"This broad, nationwide support, across party lines, is really extraordinary. I admit it humbles me, but it also emboldens me," Aigner said. "Ultimately, I want to be the candidate of this strong center."

She said the country was being attacked both from within and without, saying divisions were being stoked and consensus devalued.

"I am in politics to bridge gaps, to bring people together, and to try to reach those who might have the feeling that they are not involved. My choice of words will be clear and easy to understand. A hallmark of my entire political career has been a closeness to ordinary people and that is not going to change," she said.

How did Aigner come to be nominated?

Aigner's chances at the nomination had been gathering momentum for some time now, with various government politicians including Chancellor Merz saying they'd favor a female candidate.

The CSU had in particular lobbied for the 13th post-war German president to be the first one from the Bavarian party and the first woman.

Reports that Merz would suggest Aigner as a candidate to the steering committee first emerged on Friday, and were then confirmed by participants when the party leadership convened for two days of talks on Sunday. 

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second five-year term comes to an end next March. The special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects a German president therefore convenes in late January to choose his successor. 

The committee — comprising 1,260 people in all — is made up of federal and state lawmakers, and sometimes municipal officials and others from public life.

SPD leader and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has voiced support for her nomination.

The CDU/CSU and SPD command a majority in the committee, and it's also possible that Green party politicians might support Aigner. This means her chances of selection seem strong, at least barring unexpected developments.

Who is Ilse Aigner?

Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.

Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.

She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

She's currently the speaker or president of the state legislature in Bavaria, a role she has held since 2018.

entries.title: EU aims to pick new ECB chief by year-end
entries.summary: Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.
entries.content:
Europe

EU seeks to pick new ECB head by year end: Eurogroup chief said

November 9, 2026

Christine Lagarde's decision to step down early as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of December.

The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, announced on October 29 that she is stepping down from the position prematurely, nine months ⁠before ⁠the end of her term.

Lagarde's decision to step down early makes the schedule tight for EU leaders because they must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board ​within months.

"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in ​the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.

Who are the candidates?

The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International ​Settlements, Pablo ‌Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.

The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.

Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'

Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position," referring to his long-standing experience.

"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfill this position."

Heinen also ​said countries should ‌not see the ECB leadership contest as ​one between northern ⁠and southern European countries, or as ⁠an "​opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.

A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel ‌Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, ​whose term ends ⁠in May 2027.

The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the ⁠main eurozone countries — ​France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.

The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.

"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.

Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.

"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

entries.title: Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters
entries.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believes she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

What have Nvidia, US government said?

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Why it matters for Nvidia

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Tangled China-Nvidia web

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-licence review. Beijing has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials, who fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost their domestic AI sector, lead to their AI models catching up with the leading US models, and end up being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

What China hopes to gain

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductorspointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Edited by: Nik Martin

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

entries.title: Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?
entries.summary: She would be the first female president and the first Christian Social Union politician to hold Germany's highest office. Ilse Aigner is the favored candidate for the Federal Convention vote on January 30.
entries.content:
Germany

Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?

November 9, 2026

She would be the first female president and the first Christian Social Union politician to hold Germany's highest office. Ilse Aigner is the favored candidate for the Federal Convention vote on January 30.

Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner has emerged as the leading candidate to succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as president of Germany, a largely ceremonial office, but who is the head of state and regarded as a moral authority for the nation.

News emerged over the weekend that Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader Friedrich Merz favored Aigner, a veteran of the CDU's sister-party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and currently president of the Bavarian parliament. 

A specially convened assembly, the Federal Convention, will gather on January 30, 2027, to elect the next German president. Since the CDU, CSU, and their coalition partner the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have a majority in the convention, Aigner's election is considered highly likely.

An electrician who knows how to network

Aigner is in many respects an unusual politician, especially in Germany, where a law degree often seems to be a prerequisite for a political career. The 61-year-old has no university degree at all, though she did train as a telecommunications technician to join her parents' electrical business.

She spent several years working for the military helicopter company Eurocopter, since bought by the aviation and defense giant Airbus, where she developed electrical components.

Aigner entered the Bavarian parliament for the CSU in 1994 and then served from 1998 to 2013 in Germany's federal parliament, the Bundestag. From 2008 to 2013, she was agriculture and consumer protection minister under then Chancellor Angela Merkel.

Both of these portfolios come with considerable pressure from the public, especially during food scandals, and from powerful lobbying organizations, as well as conflicts at EU level. Aigner navigated this period without any major crises and was generally well regarded.

The personnel policies of political parties can often seem like a game of chess. In 2013, Aigner left national politics and moved back to her home state to serve as Bavaria's economy minister under then State Premier Horst Seehofer, who tried to establish her as his successor.

Colleagues and competitors: Söder and Aigner

But then came Markus Söder, at the time Bavaria's finance minister and for a long time Seehofer's biggest rival inside the CSU. It was Söder, a colorful character who also harbored pretensions to be German chancellor, who won out in the power struggle that followed Seehofer's retirement and became Bavarian state premier in 2018.

Aigner and Söder both entered Bavaria's state parliament in 1994, when they were the state's two youngest lawmakers, and their political paths have been intertwined since. Though Söder's rise to power prevented Aigner from becoming state premier, she has served as president of Bavaria's state parliament for the past eight years, and is a highly respected authority figure in the state.

For months now, Aigner has been named as a potential candidate for Germany's head of state after Steinmeier's constitutionally-enforced exit next year.

Söder himself openly mentioned her as a suitable candidate back in April, and there have been indications of support from several CDU and CSU representatives, but also from the ranks of the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But Merz seemed wary for a long time. Other names came — and went.

When the chancellor greeted Aigner by name in his opening remarks to a CSU meeting in Munich in October, he had to pause for thunderous applause from the delegates, who rose to their feet to celebrate the veteran politician.

In January, the Bavarian Merkur newspaper reported on Aigner's visit to a school in the town of Tegernsee, where she answered questions from fourth graders for their student newspaper. The CSU politician told them that she had not planned her career, but she was never able to "keep her mouth shut" and this was also part of why she had been elected to her various offices.

However, it was also noticeable that she was entirely capable of "keeping her mouth shut" when it was judicious to do so: She has largely refrained from commenting publicly during the internal maneuvering for the candidacy within the Union parties.

Aigner would not only be Germany's first female president, but also the first to be single and never married. Though men have dominated the office, there have been female nominees in almost every election since 1999. That year, the Union put forward Thuringian physicist Dagmar Schipanski, while the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), precursor to the socialist Left Party, put forward theologian Uta Ranke-Heinemann in the race against Social Democrat Johannes Rau.

But considering the majority needed in the Federal Convention, both were effectively just token candidates from minority parties, as have been all the other female candidates since. That's one reason why there has been pressure to finally choose a woman as the majority candidate. Aigner has long enjoyed respect from the conservative camp.

Too much Bavaria in Berlin?

Germany has never had a president, or indeed a chancellor, from the CSU, a regional party that nevertheless wields national power thanks to its alliance with the CDU. One CSU lawmaker, Richard Stücklen, spent four years as president of the Bundestag — formally the country's second-highest office — from 1979.

If the door to the presidency does open for Aigner, many believe it would shut out Söder's ambitions to become chancellor. The CDU — a much bigger conservative party — usually overrules the CSU when it comes to choosing a chancellor candidate when the general election comes around, and it seems unlikely that the CDU would tolerate two CSU figures leading the country.

But Aigner's election would also remove one of Söder's key rivals back home: Aigner, still only 61, enjoys excellent popularity ratings and is considered a natural rival to the 59-year-old state premier.

Ultimately, by nominating Aigner, Merz is also paving the way for someone from the CDU to become the next chancellor — provided the CDU/CSU wins the next federal election, of course.

But first, the Federal Convention must make its decision on January 30. The new German president will officially assume office in mid-March.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Turkey pushes for transition at COP31 as coal burns
entries.summary: The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.
entries.content:
November 9, 2026

The host of this year's UN climate summit remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels as it tries to inspire a global switch to clean energy.

As Turkey welcomes delegates to the 2026 UN climate talks in Antalya and pushes for cuts in global greenhouse gas emissions, it can point to surging renewable energy capacity at home. 

The COP31 host has approved more than 33 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage projects since 2022 that can power over 27 million homes.

Among the largest battery project pipelines in Europe, this storage will complement fast-expanding wind and solar energy that today provides 22% of electricity in Turkey, up from 4.5% a decade ago.

Yet this clean energy upswing is a long way from compensating for the country's overreliance on fossil fuels.

Turkey's coal-fired electricity generation increased by roughly one-third in the last decade, and in 2024 overtook Germany and Poland, which previously had the highest coal power capacity in Europe before it began to decline.

Coal undermining climate ambition

Turkey is among the few industrialized countries that has yet to commit to a phaseout date for coal — the fossil fuel with the highest planet-heating emissions.

Yet at the same time, "coal's position in the electricity market in Turkey is increasingly precarious," Efe Baysal, Turkey team lead at global environment network, 350.org, told DW.

He points to high local community opposition to coal projects on environmental grounds or due to lack of financial viability. According to German nonprofit climate campaigners, Beyond Fossil Fuels, some 97% of new coal projects have been cancelled in the last decade in Turkey, in what it calls "a global record."

"Turkey's coal project failure rate is the final nail in Europe's coal coffin," said Kasia Szeniawska of Beyond Fossil Fuels in a statement earlier this year. "Coal power is finished: it's financially risky, increases costs for billpayers, harms people's health, and sabotages climate goals."

But in June, Turkey announced plans to expand one of its largest coal plants and near double its capacity.

The move underlines Turkey's "conservative energy policy" and "highly insufficient" climate goals, said Umit Sahin, head of the climate change program at the Istanbul Policy Center, a global research institute.

Turkey's current climate target allows emissions to keep rising until 2038, meaning it will struggle to meet its plans to reach net zero by 2053, notes Climate Action Tracker, a climate research think tank.

Push for electrification, energy independence

Aside from climate concerns, Turkey's high dependence on imported fossil energy makes it extremely vulnerable to volatile global oil and gas markets. The nation currently imports 95% of its natural gas, 83% of crude oil and 60% of its coal — which together make up a "lion's share" of Turkey's energy capacity, said Baysal. 

It is partly this dependence that has inspired Turkey's push for greater electrification at the COP31 climate conference.

In September, the country launched the "35x35" global electrification pledge, which aims to increase electrification of world economies from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

The goal is for electrification to replace fossil fuels, including in transport, buildings and industry, and preferably using clean energy, though this is not mandatory —heat pumps, for example, emit fewer greenhouse gases than gas boilers, even when the electricity is generated using fossil fuels. 

The pledge complements existing UN climate goals of doubling energy efficiency and tripling renewables to keep temperature rise in line with the Paris climate agreement.

Turkey COP31 President Murat Kurum will promote the 35x35 pledge in Antalya on both climate and energy security grounds.

"[The war in the Gulf] has shown us, once again, that fossil fuels do not guarantee energy supply security," he said earlier this year at a UN climate meeting in Bonn, Germany. "Investment in alternative energy sources, in particular to support energy diversity, means stability, resilience and clean development."

But despite the rhetoric, Climate Action Tracker says that under Turkey's National Energy Plan, the COP31 host is only on track to electrify around 25% of total energy consumption by 2035.

Can renewables expansion turn the tide?

Turkey is one of numerous Mediterranean countries facing extreme climate impacts like wildfires and record heat, in addition to recent severe and deadly flooding.

As it hosts this year's climate summit, the country has a great opportunity to hasten the energy transition, said Baysal, especially since it receives nearly double the annual sunlight of Germany.

Turkey is already starting to realize some of this potential, with one analysis showing the country produces more solar module manufacturing capacity than several major European countries combined.

Solar increased from around 0.1% of total installed electricity capacity in 2014 to almost 21% at the beginning of 2026, according to Turkey's resources and energy ministry.

The COP31 host can reduce its emissions 35% by 2035 if 10 GW of solar and wind is added each interim year — as opposed to the government's target of 8 GW — noted Umit Sahin. This goal will be helped by fast-expanding battery capacity, he said.

"But if you don't phase out coal, your emissions cannot go down," he added. 

Meanwhile, the COP presidency could be a "turning point" and "a very important step for Turkey," said Sahin.

If the country wants to show climate leadership, and reduce energy dependency, it will need to embrace a "progressive climate policy" that promotes a full energy transition, he added.

Serdar Vardar and Jonathan Rampley-Sturgeon contributed reporting to this article.

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Germany news: Germany marks fateful date of November 9
entries.summary: Germany is commemorating the Nazi-led November pogroms 88 years ago. Events are also being held to mark the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Germany marks fateful date of November 9

Published November 9, 2026last updated November 9, 2026

Germany is commemorating the Nazi-led November pogroms 88 years ago. Events are also being held to mark the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Various events are being held nationwide to mark the anniversary of the November pogroms of 1938, in which dozens of Jewish people were killed
  • The opening of the Berlin Wall in 1989, which ultimately led to German reunification, is also being commemorated
  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats are set to officially nominate Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner as presidential candidate
  • The trial against eight suspected members of the militant neo-Nazi group "Saxon Separatists" is to continue in Dresden

This is a roundup of the stories from and about Germanyhitting the headlines on Monday, November 9, 2026:

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Who is Ilse Aigner, Germany's potential next president?

IN DEPTH: Who is Ilse Aigner, Germany's potential next president?

Bavarian lawmaker Ilse Aigner looks set to become Germany's first female president, with support expressed by all coalition parties and the opposition Greens.

But she would also represent a first for German in other ways, as this DW portrait article shows: Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?

Skip next section CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president

CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday confirmed that they would be putting forward Ilse Aigner as a candidate to be Germany's next head of state.

Aigner's own CSU, the CDU's Bavarian sister party, already supports her candidacy — and the federal coalition partners the Social Democrats have also made clear they would endorse her nomination if the conservatives agree on it.

This means the 61-year-old has a good chance of taking up the largely ceremonial role when the special committee that elects a German president convenes in late January.

While Angela Merkel famously served as the country's most powerful politician for more than a decade, Germany has never had a female head of state.

Read our full report here.

Skip next section Hamburg's famous Miniatur Wunderland gains new attraction

Hamburg's famous Miniatur Wunderland gains new attraction

One of Germany's most popular tourist sites, the model railway system Miniatur Wunderland, has opened a new section devoted to South America after four years of construction.

Over 175 square meters (1,883 square feet) in size, the section shows, among other things, rainforests, parts of the Andes and the Atacama Desert.

It is so far the largest part of what is, according to the Guiness Book of Records, the largest model railway network in the world.

The rainforest scene is also so far the most extravagant project carried out by the operators and was constructed jointly with a family of model-builders from Buenos Aires.

The South America section was opened with a small ceremony attended by a Peruvian representatives of the Incas, who put down the last "holy" stone meant as a symbol of a link between the former Inca center of Cusco in Peru and Hamburg.

Miniatur Wunderland is run by two brothers, Frederik and Gerrit Braun, who now head a 120-person team.

It was founded in 2001.

Skip next section WATCH: Germany's fraught relationship with its flag

WATCH: Germany's fraught relationship with its flag

Germany has a complicated attitude to patriotism resulting from the aggressive and deadly nationalism that marred part of its history.

Now, national football coach Jürgen Klopp has called on the country to "reclaim its flag," triggering a debate that is additionally heated by the resurgence of the far right in the form of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

DW looks at the issues involved in this video featuring two experts:

Skip next section German exports bounce back higher than expected in September

German exports bounce back higher than expected in September

Germany's exports are continuing their uneven path to recovery, unexpectedly rising 2% on a monthly basis in September, data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed on Monday.

Economists had predicted 0.5% growth.

The September growth reverses a 0.4% decrease in August and was the quicket rise since February.

Imports also climbed, by a whole 4.2%, much surpassing the 0.6% rebound a month ago. Economists had forecast a 0.5% increase.

Exports to EU countries grew by 3.5% compared to August, and imports from these countries rose by 4.9%.

On a yearly basis, growth in exports climbed to 7.6% from 7% in August.

Annual growth in imports also jumped to 8.7% from 6.4%. Exports to the United States were 10.3% higher, data showed.

Skip next section Social Democrats' executive committee supports Aigner nomination

Social Democrats' executive committee supports Aigner nomination

The executive committee of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's conservative-led coalition government, supports the nomination of Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner as next German president, according to the AFP news agency, citing party sources.

Aigner is "an experienced, down-to-earth politician and possesses the important ability to bring together people over party and social boundaries," according to the quoted sources.

Aigner, 61, who is a member of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), already has the support of both her party and the CDU.

Members of other parties, such as the Green Party, have also said they are in favor of Aigner, who, if elected in a vote by the Federal Convention on January 30, would become Germany's first female head of state and the first CSU member in the position.

Skip next section Commemorations of Berlin Wall opening

Commemorations of Berlin Wall opening

People across Germany are remembering the events of November 9, 1989, when the Berlin Wall separating the part of the city in former communist East Germany from that in West Germany was breached, paving the way to German reunification in 1990.

One main ceremony of commemoration is to be held at the Berlin Wall Memorial in the German capital.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is also to meet with former East German civil rights activists in the Goethe House in Weimar, the birthplace and childhood home of famous German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

In the eastern city of Cottbus, the premier of the state of Brandenburg, Dietmar Woidke, is also to host a ceremony in remembrance of the events 37 years ago.

The Berlin Wall encircled West Berlin for 28 years, separating it from East Berlin and surrounding East Germany, known as the German Democratic Republic (DDR).

Its main purpose was to prevent East Germans from escaping from their repressive country to the West, though authorities in the Soviet Bloc cast it as a defense against "fascism" coming from outside.

Skip next section Trial continues of suspected neo-Nazi 'Saxon Separatist' members

Trial continues of suspected neo-Nazi 'Saxon Separatist' members

The trial of eight people suspected of belonging to a militant neo-Nazi group, the "Saxon Separatists," continues in Dresden on Monday.

The men are accused, among other things, of "preparing a traitorous endeavor" as part of their involvement with a terrorist organization.

Prosecutors believe the group, which uses the abbreviation "SS" — like that used by the paramilitary "Schutzstaffel" that operated in the Nazi era — planned to overthrow democracy in Germany, starting with an armed takeover of the eastern state of Saxony. 

The eight men were arrested in November 2024 during international raids conducted in Germany, Austria and Poland and have been remanded in custody since then.

The trial, which began in January, is scheduled to last until December

Skip next section Merz calls for defense of democracy, freedom

Merz calls for defense of democracy, freedom

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has used the November 9 anniversary of several important dates in German history to call on people in Germany and Europe to stand up for democracy and liberty.

November 9 was the day in 1918 that the monarchy fell, in 1938 a day of antisemitic violence known as the November pogroms, and in 1989 the day when the Berlin Wall opened, paving the way for the reunification of Germany.

Writing on X, Merz said, "November 9 stands for the darkest and the happiest hours of our history: for antisemitism and persecution, for the beginning of democracy and the fall of the Wall."

"Freedom and democracy can never be taken for granted. Let us defend them — in Germany and Europe," he wrote.

Skip next section Germany marks November pogroms anniversary

Germany marks November pogroms anniversary

 Commemorations are to be held nationwide to commemorate the Nazi pogroms of November 9-10, 1938, when mobs went on an antisemitic rampage, killing at least 91 Jewish people, ransacking Jewish businesses and burning down hundreds of synagogues.

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to attend events in the eastern city of Weimar, where he is due to lay a wreath and hold a speech at the memorial site established at the site of the former Nazi concentration camp of Buchenwald.

The Jüdische Gemeinde zu Berlin is to have all the names of Jewish Nazi victims read out over the day in commemoration of the pogroms.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will be attending a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue in Munich, which was opened 68 years to the day after the main synagogue in the city was destroyed in the pogroms. 

The pogroms are sometimes known as "Reichskristallnacht" or "Night of Broken Glass," but this name has fallen out of favor as underplaying the horrors of what happened.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

November 9 is known as the "day of destiny" in Germany, a day that has in the past seen both horrific events and others that have shaped the country in a more positive way.

Into the first category come the November pogroms of 1938, in which the Nazi regime unleashed a wave of antisemitic violence that led to the deaths of dozens of Jewish people and the burning of hundreds of synagogues.

Events will be held nationwide to commemorate the 88th anniversary of the pogroms, including some in Weimar attended by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will also attend a ceremony marking the 20th anniversary of the Ohel Jakob Main Synagogue, which opened 68 years to the day after the destruction of Munich's main synagogue in the pogroms.

But November 9, 1989, also saw the opening of the Berlin Wall, when thousands of East Berliners unexpectedly crossed into the west of the city, an event that eventually led to the reunification of Germany.

Read on here for more on these and other stories connected with Europe's largest economy.

entries.title: India news: Delhi air quality level 'severe' after Diwali
entries.summary: Illegal fireworks during Diwali celebrations have impacted New Delhi's air quality level. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India news: Delhi air quality level 'severe' after Diwali

Published November 9, 2026last updated November 9, 2026

Illegal fireworks during Diwali celebrations have impacted New Delhi's air quality level. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is our rolling coverage from India on Monday, November 9:

  • Delhi's air quality has significantly worsened as Diwali celebrations saw people violating a ban on conventional firecrackers
  • Smog has engulfed the Indian capital's roads and high-rises, reducing visibility
  • One locality reportedly witnessed PM 2.5 levels rising to over 58 times the WHO recommended daily limit

Skip next section Ousted Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina seeks new passport in sign of return from India exile

Ousted Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina seeks new passport in sign of return from India exile

Former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been in a self-imposed exile in India since her 2024 ouster, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her planned return to Bangladesh, reports said Monday.

Lawyers at London-based firm Matrix Chambers, representing Hasina, have reportedly written to Bangladesh’s embassy in New Delhi, seeking the fresh documents.

"In view of the reported revocation of her existing Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card (NID) by the Interim Government and other authorities, I respectfully request that you take the necessary steps to ​issue a new Bangladeshi passport and National Identity Card for our client," Reuters cited the letter addressed to the diplomatic mission as saying.

The letter urged for the applications to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of Hasina's Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments."

The Bangladeshi government, however, said it does not provide "passport to a terrorist."

Hasina had earlier said that she wants to return to Bangladesh —  where she has been sentenced to death in absentia for ordering a deadly crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising —  in December at any cost.

Bangladesh’s government has been seeking her extradition from India.

"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with ⁠India. We want her handed over," Bangladesh state minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told ​the media.

The ties between between the two South Asian neighbors took a hit after Hasina resigned and fled to India aboard a military helicopter amid deadly mass protests against her government.

Skip next section WATCH — India's AI ambitions and its quest to become a global tech superpower

WATCH — India's AI ambitions and its quest to become a global tech superpower

India wants to become one of the world's leading artificial intelligence (AI) powers by 2047. 

Both opportunities and challenges lie ahead to achieve that goal.

As ChatGPT, Google Gemini and domestic AI platforms compete for a share of one of the world's largest digital markets, India's government is investing billions of dollars in AI infrastructure, research and startups.

With a population of 1.4 billion people, vast linguistic diversity and a fast-growing technology sector, the country could play a major role in the future of artificial intelligence.

Yet questions remain over foreign investment, dependence on US tech giants, patent output and the ongoing brain drain of top talent. Can India turn its AI ambitions into global leadership?



Find out more in this report:

Skip next section 19 Indian seafarers evacuated from Yemen

19 Indian seafarers evacuated from Yemen

Nineteen Indian seafarers who had been stranded in Yemen's Hodeidah and Sanaa for nearly two weeks have been evacuated, the Indian Embassy in Yemen said in a post on X late Sunday.

The embassy added that the sailors were in good health and on their way back to India.

A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in Yemen's longstanding conflict crumbled  in July, restarting fighting between the Houthi rebels and the Middle Eastern country's Saudi Arabia-backed government. 

According to India's foreign ministry, 23 Indian nationals have been killed since the Middle East war began in February, with seafarers accounting for 15 deaths.

Skip next section Delhi air pollution worsens as firecracker ban defied on Diwali

Delhi air pollution worsens as firecracker ban defied on Diwali

Residents of New Delhi and nearby areas have woken up breathing, or rather choking on, smoke and fine particulate matter, as revelers celebrating the Hindu festival of Diwali disregarded a firecracker ban, adding to the ongoing pollution crisis that grips the capital in the winter months. 

Several parts of New Delhi and the surrounding satellite cities that make up the National Capital Region (NCR), have reported an Air Quality Index (AQI) in the "severe" category, posing significant health risks.

Skies over the capital which were lit up by fireworks on Sunday night are now blanketed with a thick layer of toxic smog.

Air pollution in parts of Delhi-NCR dangerously surpassed the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended 24-hour average limit on Monday by over 50 times, reports said.

IQair, that cites data from a government monitoring station in the city, put the level of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles at 879 micrograms per cubic meter in Delhi's central Mandir Marg area early on Monday, news agency AFP reported, which comes up to nearly 59 times the WHO limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter.

New Delhi is one of the world's most polluted capitals. The city has for many years witnessed a recurring winter smog fueled by vehicular emission, crop-residue fires in neighboring states and industrial activity. 

Millions of people celebrate Diwali with fireworks in the smog season, releasing massive amounts of fine particles — PM2.5 and PM10 — and soot in the already compromised air.

On Saturday, Delhi witnessed the worst air on Diwali eve in a decade. 

Last month, India's top court had restricted conventional firecrackers, allowing only "green firecrackers" in three-hour timeframes on Saturday and Sunday. But the Supreme Court's ban failed to hold.

"Green firecrackers" are designed to produce lower air and noise pollution but still emit 65 to 70% of conventional firecracker pollution.

A series of winter pollution rules had also come into effect in New Delhi from November 1, including vehicle restrictions and construction bans.

Air pollution has been a Gordian knot for successive Delhi governments who blame each other for failing to tackle the issue.

But a long-term solution to curb New Delhi's air pollution crisis remains elusive.



Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia,from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our Monday digest of all the news, events and trends that are making a splash in India.

The morning after Diwali — the festival of lights — has left the Indian capital shrouded in toxic smog as people flouted a firecracker ban in large numbers, exacerbating the city's seasonal pollution conditions.

Several parts of New Delhi and its surrounding regions are choking with the Air Quality Index (AQI) in the "severe" range.

As I write this, I can still hear crackers going off intermittently well into the Monday morning — the popping sound making me check the AQI indicator on the air purifier next to me, every time.

In other news, 19 Indian seafarers stranded in Yemen's Hodeidah and Sanaa for the last two weeks have been evacuated and are on their way back to their home country.

Stay tuned as we bring you all this and more.
